newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS - Norway govt sticks to tight line in budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Norway govt sticks to tight line in budget.

text.p: Norway's Labour government stuck to its guns on Friday and maintained a restrictive fiscal policy in its final 1997 budget proposal despite political pressure to raise public spending in line with burgeoning state coffers.
The Finance Ministry said it wanted to keep a tight grip on the money purse to restrain price and wage inflation.
"Current indicators point to a somewhat stronger growth in GDP and employment than projected in the National Budget at the beginning of October," a statement from the ministry said.
"In order to counteract inflationary developments, the government now proposes a tighter fiscal policy than proposed in the National Budget."

Analysts said the government, which took office at the end of October, had shown strength by sticking to its policy despite hostile opposition parties, which called for increased spending partly through higher welfare payments and tax revisions.
"The government has shown restraint and skill in manoeuvring in parliament and has put forward a good fiscal policy," said Olav Rune Oeverland, chief analyst at Den norske Bank.

"Finance Minister (Jens) Stoltenberg has shown a will to force through a tight budget, which is central to the long-term perspective in light of the growing surplus. It should be positive for the financial markets."
The ministry said it had revised upwards expectations for next year's budget surplus to 55.4 billion crowns ($8.64 billion) from 40.9 billion crowns in the draft budget document.
The surplus, which was expected to be around 45.7 billion crowns in 1996 compared with previous projections of 37.9 billion crowns, has swollen as oil prices have soared to five year highs.
Norway produces more than three million barrels per day of oil and is the world's second largest exporter after Saudi Arabia.

The ministry said the surplus amounted to 6.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 -- the Maastrict convergence criteria for joining Economic and Monetary Union in 1999 require that a budget deficit does not fall below three percent of GDP.
Forecasts for growth in consumer prices in 1996 and 1997 were left unchanged from the October draft at 1.25 percent and 2.5 percent, respectively.

Overall GDP was estimated to grow by 3.1 percent in 1997, against 5.4 percent in 1996, while mainland GDP, which excludes the offshore oil and gas sector, was forecast to rise by 2.5 percent next year.
The ministry said the current account surplus would amount to 82 billion crowns in 1997 against 77.6 billion crowns in 1996, based on an oil price of 125 crowns per barrel in 1997.
